concepts.title: Cognitive debt
concepts.definition: **Cognitive debt** is the accumulating deficit in a person's own cognitive engagement, memory formation, and sense of ownership that builds when mental work is habitually offloaded to an external aid such as an LLM: the work still gets done, but the neural and behavioral capacity it would have exercised goes progressively under-used, and the shortfall compounds across sessions rather than resetting when the tool is put away.
concepts.explanation: The term comes from a four-month MIT Media Lab EEG study of essay writing (arXiv 2506.08872), a single 54-participant preprint rather than a replicated literature, so the evidence is suggestive, not settled. Its core mechanism is that cognitive activity scales down in proportion to external support: participants wrote under LLM, search-engine, or no-tool conditions for three sessions, and EEG brain connectivity ordered the groups brain-only strongest, search intermediate, LLM weakest, while LLM users also produced more homogeneous essays, reported the lowest ownership of their text, and often failed to quote sentences they had just written — evidence that offloading composition weakens encoding at the moment of writing. The crossover fourth session is what makes it debt rather than a transient mode: participants who had written with the LLM and then lost it stayed under-engaged (reduced alpha and beta connectivity), whereas participants who had worked unaided and only then received the LLM showed higher recall and engagement comparable to search users. Ordering matters — unaided effort first builds capacity that tool-first work never establishes.
key_properties: EEG connectivity during writing ordered brain-only > search engine > LLM
LLM users reported the lowest essay ownership and frequently could not quote their own just-written text
Crossover result: LLM-to-brain writers remained under-engaged; brain-to-LLM writers retained higher recall and engagement
Effects accumulated over four months and three sessions, then showed in a fourth crossover session
Evidence base is one 54-participant study (18 in the crossover), an arXiv preprint

relationships.clause: describes how retained material decays without review, while cognitive debt names the upstream failure — offloaded work is weakly encoded in the first place, so there is less for the curve to act on

concepts.applications: Sequencing AI assistance in education and onboarding so that unaided work comes before model help; justifying AI-use policies that preserve deliberate practice on tasks where the human must retain the skill or the content.
